mcqs.question: A `withdraw()` method has different behavior for a valid amount, a negative amount, and an amount exceeding the balance. How many unit tests should this ideally produce?
options: One test covering all three cases with three separate assertion blocks
Three separate tests, one per behavior, since each is a distinct case with its own failure reason
Two tests: one for the valid case and one combined test for both error cases
One test per line of the withdraw() implementation
mcqs.explanation: Each scenario is a distinct behavior with its own reason to fail, so splitting them keeps a red build immediately readable — one failing test name tells you exactly which case broke. Bundling them into one test reintroduces the ambiguity the one-behavior-per-test principle exists to avoid.

mcqs.question: A test opens a real network connection to an external API and takes 3 seconds to run. Which FIRST properties does this most directly violate?
options: Self-checking and Timely
Isolated only, since network calls don't affect test speed
None, as long as the assertion is correct
Fast and Repeatable — it's slow and its outcome depends on network availability and external state
mcqs.explanation: A real network call is slow (violating Fast) and its result depends on external factors like connectivity or the API's live state (violating Repeatable) — the same call could pass in one environment and fail in another with no code change.

mcqs.question: A test reaches into a private method to verify the exact internal call order a function uses to compute its result. What is the main risk of this approach?
options: It makes the test run slower than asserting on the public output
It violates the FIRST principle of being self-checking
It couples the test to the current implementation, so it breaks on any internal refactor even if behavior is unchanged
It has no real risk, since testing internals gives stronger guarantees than testing outputs
mcqs.explanation: Asserting on internal call order couples the test to implementation details rather than the observable contract, so a harmless refactor that doesn't change behavior can still turn the test red — the defining symptom of a brittle, implementation-coupled test.

mcqs.question: After renaming a private helper method with no change in output, five unrelated tests fail. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The tests are brittle — they're coupled to implementation details rather than observable behavior
The tests are correctly catching a real regression
The test suite violates the Timely property of FIRST
The renamed method must have introduced a hidden bug
mcqs.explanation: If behavior genuinely didn't change but tests still fail after an internal rename, the tests were asserting on implementation shape rather than outputs a caller would observe — the textbook definition of brittleness, not a real regression.

mcqs.question: A test asserts five unrelated facts about an order and fails on the first assertion. What problem does this illustrate, and why does it matter?
options: Assertion roulette — you only learn about the first failure and must fix and rerun repeatedly to discover the rest
A violation of the Isolated FIRST principle, since assertions share state
It's not a problem; frameworks report all failing assertions in one test regardless of order
Test-induced design damage, since the order object has too many fields
mcqs.explanation: Most frameworks stop at the first failing assertion, so bundling five checks into one test hides whether the other four would also fail — you discover them one rerun at a time. Splitting into one test per behavior surfaces every real failure immediately.
